about.name: Habit library
about.whatThisIs: Evidence-graded habits for six life areas. Each habit has one fixed core (never changes), three starting levels (light, standard, full), an example if-then, notes that fit it to a person's life, safety notes, and the studies behind it.
about.howToUse: Pick from the habits listed under the goal that matches the person's goal (goals[].habits, in order of fit; step 1 = can start now, step 2 = later). Support habits help any goal in that area. Fit delivery, time and place with fitNotes; never change the core. If none fits, write your own and mark it as not from the library.
about.grades: How strong the evidence is that the core works: A strongest, then B, C, D thinnest. Rx means it is only run with a clinician. Each grade was checked against the studies' full texts where they were available (Sept 2026).
about.effort: effort 1 to 3: how much it takes to start (1 = easy to start, 2 = more effort or a structured program, 3 = an intensive program).
about.drivers: Why the area is hard for the person: control (not in control), skill (don't feel good at it), alone (doing it alone), room (no room for it), unclear (don't know what I want). A habit's drivers are the reasons it fits best.
about.conditions: when/unless use the keys in fields. A value can be one option or a list (any match). {rule: '...'} is the library's own code for a condition that needs more than one field; read it as a description. Keys that are not in fields describe the GOAL, not the person: goalKinds, want, shape, stage and focus are read off the goal the habit would serve; fn holds the library's own code and the app treats it as a description until it is written into the choice. unless is a condition that cancels the when; it may be a list, any one of which cancels.
about.internalOnly: grade, evidence and sources are for choosing, never shown to the person.
about.levelShape: Each level is {text, times, minutes}: text is the level in the person's words; times is how many times a week (a number, 0.5 for every two weeks, 0.25 for monthly), or 'daily', or 'once' for a thing set up one time; minutes is one time's length. Drafted by a session from the text on 29 Sep 2026 for the owner's redlines; they size the stones on the sand and count against the bad week, and are never shown as text.

caffeine.name: Caffeine cut-off
caffeine.promise: I'll keep caffeine away from my sleep, so my sleep is actually mine.
caffeine.core: Pick a last-caffeine time, counted back from your main sleep, and hold it. Energy drinks count too.

light.text: Caffeine-free for the 8 hours before your main sleep.

standard.text: Last coffee 9 hours before your main sleep; last energy drink 12 hours before.

full.text: Last coffee 9 hours before sleep, energy drinks 12, and up to about 400 mg a day (four cups).

caffeine.ifThenExample: When I hit my cut-off time, I switch to water or decaf.

ifThenExamplesFor.text: When I take my mid-shift break, I have my last caffeine of the night.
When I finish lunch, I call that my last coffee.

fitNotes.text: Count back from your main sleep, whatever the hour. Your last energy drink goes at the mid-shift break, not the end.
Try front-loading: have the afternoon coffee before 2 p.m.
Keep the evening cup, make it decaf: same ritual, no caffeine.
Swap energy drinks for water and you keep the money and the sleep.

caffeine.evidence: In a meta-analysis of 24 studies (healthy adults), caffeine cut total sleep by about 45 minutes and sleep efficiency by 7%. From the pooled dose-response, a regular cup of coffee (about 107 mg) needs about 9 hours before bed and a standard serve of pre-workout supplement (about 218 mg) about 13 hours to leave total sleep time untouched. Mostly small lab studies.

sources.cite: Gardiner et al. 2023, Sleep Medicine Reviews: caffeine and subsequent sleep, meta-analysis of 24 studies

sleep.name: Steady sleep times
sleep.promise: I'll give my body a rhythm it can count on.
sleep.core: Keep your bedtime and wake time steady, weekends included. You pick the times.

light.text: The same wake time on workdays; within an hour of it on days off.

standard.text: Bed and wake times within the same 30 minutes every day.

full.text: Bed and wake times within 30 minutes every day, plus daylight within an hour of waking.

levels.light: Bed 20 minutes earlier on the nights you can. Your wake time stays where it is.
levels.standard: Bed 20 minutes earlier, then another 20 once that holds, with a steady wake time.
levels.full: Bedtime earlier in 20-minute steps toward 7 hours, a steady wake time, and daylight soon after waking.

sleep.ifThenExample: When I hear my alarm, I get up and open the curtains.

ifThenExamplesFor.text: When I finish my shift, I set the same wake time as last time and close the curtains.
When I reach 20 minutes before my usual bedtime, I start getting into bed.
When I finish settling the house for the night, I set my own alarm for my usual wake time.
When I close the laptop for the night, I set the same alarm as every day.

fitNotes.text: After night shifts, anchor to your main sleep block, even if it starts at 9 a.m. Hold it on days off where you can.
When care breaks up your nights, hold the wake time on nights without duty; if another adult lives with you, trade night duty.
Later body clocks are normal at this age. Pick later times you can also hold on weekends.
Under six hours? Start with an earlier bedtime, 20 minutes at a time. Your wake time stays where it is.
A cheap alarm clock does the job; no sleep gadgets needed.

notFor.reason: With rotating or on-call nights, fixed times can't hold for you, so the wind-down habit and its night-shift lens look after your sleep instead.

sleep.evidence: In 60,977 UK Biobank adults whose sleep was measured by a week of wrist-accelerometer wear and who were then followed for about 6 years, everyone above the least regular fifth had 20–30% lower mortality after full adjustment, and regularity predicted death better than sleep length. Observational.

sources.cite: Windred et al. 2024, SLEEP: sleep regularity and mortality, 60,977 adults

outofbed.name: Out of bed if awake
outofbed.promise: When sleep won't come, I'll get up instead of fighting it, so my bed goes back to meaning sleep.
outofbed.core: Awake for about 20 minutes? Get up, and come back only when sleepy, so your bed stays for sleep.

light.text: Get up after about 30 minutes awake.

standard.text: Get up after about 20 minutes awake.

full.text: Get up after about 20 minutes, and keep screens and reading out of bed.

outofbed.ifThenExample: When I notice I've been awake a while, I get up and go to the chair.

fitNotes.text: No other room? A chair in the same room works, in dim light.
Skip it on nights you're on duty.

outofbed.evidence: Across 80 insomnia-treatment studies (15,351 people), stimulus control was among the three most effective CBT-I components, alongside sleep restriction and cognitive therapy. It lengthened total sleep time, but on its own it didn't significantly lower insomnia severity. Results varied a lot between studies.

sources.cite: 2024 component network meta-analysis of CBT-I, 80 studies (Clinical Psychology Review)

cbti.name: A CBT-I sleep program
cbti.promise: I'll retrain my sleep with the program that works, not a pile of tips.
cbti.core: Work through a structured CBT-I program, by app or with a clinician, including a set sleep window.

light.text: Guided by a clinician, at your pace.

standard.text: A 6-week program, such as the free CBT-i Coach app.

full.text: A full 6 to 8 week program with a daily sleep diary.

cbti.ifThenExample: When I sit down this Sunday, I set up the program and my sleep window.

fitNotes.text: Work through it with a clinician, who can adjust the sleep window for night work.
The CBT-i Coach app is free.

notFor.reason: You've had ongoing low mood, so this one waits for a clinician to run it with you rather than alone in an app.

cbti.evidence: Across 80 studies (15,351 people), sleep restriction was the most effective CBT-I component for insomnia severity (d = −0.45), followed by cognitive therapy (d = −0.28); sleep hygiene and relaxation alone had no significant effect. Studies varied a lot and most were unblinded. Sleep restriction causes daytime sleepiness at first, so avoid driving drowsy.

sources.cite: 2024 component network meta-analysis of CBT-I, 80 studies (Clinical Psychology Review)

winddown.name: Wind-down and bedroom setup
winddown.promise: I'll wind down the same way before every sleep, so my body knows what's next.
winddown.core: Before your main sleep, phone away and the same short wind-down, in a dark, quiet room.

light.text: Phone away 15 minutes before sleep.

standard.text: Phone charging outside the bedroom 30 minutes before sleep, plus a 10-minute wind-down.

full.text: Phone out 60 minutes before sleep, and the same wind-down before every sleep, naps included.

winddown.ifThenExample: When I brush my teeth, I put my phone in its overnight spot.

ifThenExamplesFor.text: When I get home from the shift, I put the phone in its spot before I shower.
When I hear the house go quiet, I put the phone in its spot and start my wind-down.

fitNotes.text: Count back from your main sleep, whenever it falls. Blackout curtains or an eye mask stand in for night.
No spare room? Phone face-down in a drawer across the room works.
Foil or a blanket over the window works as blackout, and a cheap alarm clock replaces the phone alarm.
If your phone is a baby monitor, care alarm or on-call line, keep it on for those calls only.

winddown.evidence: In 42 RCTs (4,245 adults), insomnia severity fell about 3.4 points from before to after sleep hygiene education, but it did worse than CBT-I, exercise and other active treatments, and most trials had a high risk of bias; an 80-study CBT-I analysis found sleep hygiene had no significant effect on its own. In a 38-student pilot, putting the phone away 30 minutes before bed for 4 weeks cut time to fall asleep by about 12 minutes and added about 18 minutes of sleep (self-reported). A support habit, not a sleep treatment.

sources.cite: 2025 meta-analysis, Sleep Medicine Reviews: sleep hygiene education for insomnia, 42 RCTs
2024 component network meta-analysis of CBT-I, 80 studies (Clinical Psychology Review)
He et al. 2020, PLOS One: bedtime phone restriction pilot, n = 38

move.name: Move more each week
move.promise: I'll move a little more each week, at my pace, and feel the difference.
move.core: Build toward a weekly target you set with moderate activity: walking, cycling, swimming, anything that raises your breathing.

light.text: 10 minutes of brisk walking, 3 days a week, from wherever you start.

standard.text: About 150 minutes a week of moderate movement, in bouts of 10 minutes or more, on most days.

full.text: About 300 minutes a week of moderate movement, or half that of vigorous, spread over most days.

move.ifThenExample: When I get dressed, I head out for my session.

ifThenExamplesFor.text: When I arrive at work, I walk one lap of the block before going in.
When I finish my shift, I do my 10 minutes before I sleep.
When I finish drop-off, I do my walk before anything else.
When I finish my morning coffee, I go out for my walk.

fitNotes.text: Low-impact only: stationary bike, pool, elliptical, or flat walking if your joint is fine with it. Stop anything that causes sharp pain.
Arm-based cardio: handcycle, push intervals, swimming or wheelchair sport. The same weekly minutes count.
Pick steady-footing options: a stationary bike, a treadmill with rails, or water walking.
Only movement your surgeon or physical therapist has cleared.
Seated or water-based options count fully.
Try one session a week with others: a walking group, class or online group.
Keep most sessions at a pace you can talk at ("zone 2"), and make one a week harder.
Bring the kids along: a walk, a bike ride or a kickabout together counts.
Walk while someone else sits with them, or walk with them if they can; a slow lap together counts for both.
Indoors works: a free video, the stairs in your building, or a mall walk.
Park at the far end of the lot, or walk laps on a break.
Every 10-minute bout counts: before work, at lunch, a walk while you take a call.
Your shift is work, not the session. Ten minutes before it, at your own pace, is what counts.
Steps easier to track than minutes? Aim for about 7,000 a day, adding 1,000 at a time from wherever you start. Going from 2,000 to 4,000 already brings much of the benefit.
Walking and free videos count; no gym needed.

safety.text: Get a quick go-ahead from your doctor or physical therapist, and let them set the target.

move.evidence: Walking or jogging is among the most effective exercises for depression: a 2024 network meta-analysis of 218 RCTs (14,170 people with depression) put it near the top (g = -0.63 vs active controls), though certainty was low and only one trial was at low risk of bias. WHO sets 150–300 moderate minutes a week; across 15 cohorts, half that already went with most of the lower depression risk (observational). Counting steps instead, about 7,000 a day is the practical target, and going from 2,000 to 4,000 already gets much of the benefit (57 cohort studies).

sources.cite: Noetel et al. 2024, BMJ: exercise for depression, network meta-analysis
Bull et al. 2020, BJSM: WHO guidelines on physical activity and sedentary behaviour
Pearce et al. 2022, JAMA Psychiatry: activity dose and depression risk, 15 cohorts
Ding et al. 2025, Lancet Public Health: daily steps and health outcomes, 57 studies from 35 cohorts

strength.name: Strength training
strength.promise: I'll get stronger, one short session at a time, and feel it in everything else I do.
strength.core: Work every major muscle group against resistance, building to 2 or more days a week.

light.text: 1 session a week of 10 to 15 minutes, building to 2.

standard.text: 2 sessions a week, 15 to 20 minutes each.

full.text: 2 sessions a week, 20 to 30 minutes, adding reps or resistance every two weeks.

"3 sessions a week, with loads rising over time." : null; }
strength.ifThenExample: When I brush my teeth on a strength night, I do my circuit.

ifThenExamplesFor.text: When I start making dinner on a strength day, I do my 10-minute block first.
When I have a quiet house on a strength night, I do my circuit.
When I get ready for my shift on a strength day, I do my circuit first, not after.

fitNotes.text: Chair sit-to-stands, bands and counter push-ups load the muscles without pounding the joint. Skip any move that pinches or hurts.
Upper body and core with bands or machines, plus rotator-cuff and shoulder-blade work every session. Your shoulders do the walking, so they come first.
Lower-body and machine work first; keep overhead and gripping moves light until the shoulder or hands settle.
Healthy shoulders keep your season going: rotator-cuff and scapular work before any pressing, and a physio look if one grinds.
Hold a counter for standing moves.
Only exercises your physical therapist has cleared.
Lighter loads with steady breathing; no breath-holding.
Body weight and one resistance band are enough.
Two 10-minute blocks on the same day count as a session.

safety.text: A quick go-ahead from your doctor or physical therapist first, so you can build without guessing.

strength.evidence: In 33 RCTs (1,877 people), resistance training reduced depressive symptoms by a moderate amount (Δ = 0.66; 0.56 in blinded trials), regardless of volume or strength gained. Results varied a lot between trials (I² = 76%), with signs of publication bias. WHO recommends it on 2+ days a week for every adult.

sources.cite: Gordon et al. 2018, JAMA Psychiatry: resistance training and depressive symptoms, 33 RCTs
Bull et al. 2020, BJSM: WHO guidelines on physical activity and sedentary behaviour

balance.name: Steady on your feet
balance.promise: I'll train my balance three days a week, so I stay steady on my feet.
balance.core: Practice balance and functional moves (standing balance, sit-to-stands, heel-to-toe walking) 3 days a week.

light.text: 3 days a week, 2 minutes.

standard.text: 3 days a week, 5 to 10 minutes.

full.text: 3 days a week, 15 minutes, moving to harder stances as you steady.

balance.ifThenExample: When I put the kettle on, I do my balance moves at the counter while it boils.

fitNotes.text: Both hands on the counter; skip single-leg stands if they hurt.
A tai chi or falls-prevention class adds company.

notFor.reason: Standing balance work doesn't fit how you move, so your rehab team is the one to guide transfer and pressure-relief skills.

balance.evidence: In a Cochrane review of 108 RCTs (23,407 people over 60), exercise cut falls by 23% and the number of people falling by 15% (high certainty). Balance and functional training worked reliably, and programs adding strength work did best. Offered at 65+ or with balance concerns.

sources.cite: Sherrington et al. 2019, Cochrane: exercise for preventing falls, 108 RCTs

bodywork.name: Care for the sore spot
bodywork.promise: I'll look after the part that hurts, five minutes at a time, and keep the rest of me moving.
bodywork.core: A short set of exercises for the sore area, on a regular schedule, picked with a physio or from a reputable program. Keep the rest of you moving.

light.text: 5 minutes, 3 days a week.

standard.text: 10 minutes, most days.

full.text: 15 minutes daily, plus one general movement session a week.

bodywork.ifThenExample: When I reach for my shoes, I do my five minutes on the floor first.

ifThenExamplesFor.text: When I reach for my boots, I do my five minutes on the floor first.
When I sit down at my desk, I do my set before opening anything.
When I wake for the shift, I do my set before coffee.

fitNotes.text: For a back: hip hinges, bird-dogs, walking; lift from the hips. For a hip or knee: sit-to-stands and step-ups holding a counter.
For a shoulder or hands: rotator-cuff and shoulder-blade work with a band; grip and wrist work in short sets.
Change position every 30 minutes as well; the set is a reset, not a cure for the chair.
The set is your warm-up and protection; the work itself isn't the exercise.
Pick the set with a physio visit or a free, reputable program (a national health service or university physio site); after that it costs nothing.
Five minutes before work beats fifteen that get skipped.

safety.text: If there is new numbness or weakness, a change in bladder or bowel control, unexplained weight loss, fever with the pain, or pain that wakes you at night, get same-day care first, not a habit.
A quick go-ahead from your doctor or physical therapist first, so you can build without guessing.

bodywork.evidence: In a Cochrane review of 249 trials (24,486 people), exercise cut chronic low-back pain by about 15 points out of 100 versus no treatment, usual care or placebo (moderate certainty), but improved function only slightly, and gains were smaller against other treatments. For knee osteoarthritis, the 2024 Cochrane update (139 trials, 12,468 people) found modest gains in pain and function, with no difference between exercise types (low to moderate certainty). Most trials couldn't blind participants.

sources.cite: Hayden et al. 2021, Cochrane: exercise therapy for chronic low back pain, 249 trials, n = 24,486
Fransen et al. 2015, Cochrane: exercise for knee osteoarthritis, 54 trials
Lawford et al. 2024, Cochrane (CD004376.pub4): exercise for knee osteoarthritis, update of Fransen 2015, 139 trials, n = 12,468

sitbreaks.name: Movement breaks
sitbreaks.promise: I'll interrupt the long stretches before they wear me down.
sitbreaks.core: Break up long stretches of sitting or focused work with a few minutes away, moving if you can.

light.text: Stand and move for 2 minutes every hour.

standard.text: 2 to 3 minutes of movement every 30 minutes of sitting.

full.text: Move every 30 minutes, plus one standing or walking meeting a day.

levels.light: Sit down for 5 minutes every two hours.
levels.standard: Sit down, or shift to a different position, for 5 minutes every 90 minutes.
levels.full: Sit or shift position every 90 minutes, plus 10 minutes with your feet up after the shift.

sitbreaks.ifThenExample: When I hear my 30-minute timer, I stand and walk to refill my water.

ifThenExamplesFor.text: When I've been on my feet for two hours, I sit down for five minutes.

fitNotes.text: Standing, gentle marching or a lap of the room counts.
Every break is a pressure relief: lift, lean or tilt for 1 to 2 minutes, then a lap of the room.
On a standing job, flip it: sit down for five minutes every two hours. The habit is the break, not the standing.
Try a repeating timer, and take calls standing.
Worth asking for a sit-stand desk: in workplace trials, desks cut sitting about twice as much as reminders alone.
Tie it to TV or reading: move at every episode or chapter break.

sitbreaks.evidence: In a meta-analysis of 22 samples (2,335 people, about half of them students), micro-breaks of up to 10 minutes raised vigor (d = 0.36) and cut fatigue (d = 0.35), but didn't reliably boost performance. In 30 lab crossover trials (653 adults), light or moderate activity breaks lowered post-meal blood sugar more than standing breaks did; these were single-session tests, so long-term metabolic benefit isn't proven. Workplace programs cut sitting by up to 28 minutes a day with reminders and about 64 minutes with sit-stand desks.

sources.cite: Albulescu et al. 2022, PLOS One: micro-breaks meta-analysis, 22 samples
2020 network meta-analysis: interrupting prolonged sitting, 30 crossover trials
Virtanen et al. 2025, Lancet Public Health: workplace health promotion, 88 meta-analyses

seated.name: Sit down to eat
seated.promise: I'll sit down and actually eat my meals, like someone who deserves a meal.
seated.core: Meals sitting down, on a plate, screens off; nothing eaten standing or off someone else's plate.

light.text: One seated, screen-free meal a day.

standard.text: Every main meal seated and plated; nothing eaten standing.

full.text: Every main meal seated and plated, and the fork goes down between bites.

seated.ifThenExample: When I have food ready, I put it on a plate and sit before the first bite.

fitNotes.text: Plate your own portion before serving the kids; leftovers go in a box, not your mouth.
A 15-minute seated staff meal counts; put it on the schedule like a shift.
A break-room chair and a real plate count; a bar stool at the counter does not.
A table for one, phone across the room.

seated.evidence: In a meta-analysis of 24 lab studies, eating while distracted raised how much people ate at the meal (moderately) and even more at later meals, while remembering what you ate cut later intake; paying closer attention during the meal did not change that meal. Short-term lab studies, mostly in young students, with no long-term weight trials.

sources.cite: Robinson et al. 2013, AJCN: eating attentively, systematic review and meta-analysis of 24 studies

plants.name: More plants on the plate
plants.promise: I'll build my meals around food that feeds me.
plants.core: Build meals around plants: vegetables or fruit at every meal, plus beans, whole grains, nuts and olive oil in place of ultra-processed food.

light.text: Add a vegetable or fruit to one meal a day.

standard.text: Vegetables or fruit at every meal, plus beans or whole grains once a day.

full.text: The full pattern: plants at every meal, beans, whole grains, nuts and olive oil daily, ultra-processed food rarely.

plants.ifThenExample: When I plate a meal, I add the vegetable first.

ifThenExamplesFor.text: When I take my meal break, I put the vegetable on the plate first.

fitNotes.text: Frozen and canned vegetables, dried beans and oats count and cost less.
Pre-cut vegetables, bagged salad and batch-cooked beans count.
Pack meals for the shift, so the vending machine is the backup, not the default.
Try one plant-based dish the whole household shares.

plants.evidence: In 16 RCTs (45,826 people, mostly without diagnosed depression), improving diet reduced depressive symptoms slightly (g = 0.28; 0.17 vs active controls), with no effect on anxiety. Results varied a lot between trials (I² = 89%), with signs of small-study bias, and the benefit showed in female but not male samples. Graded on this mental-health evidence only.

sources.cite: Firth et al. 2019, Psychosomatic Medicine: dietary improvement and depression, 16 RCTs

alcohol.name: Alcohol-free days
alcohol.promise: I'll drink on my own terms, with a cap I choose and nights that are mine.
alcohol.core: Pick a cap you can keep, build in nights without drinking, and keep count. You set the numbers.

light.text: One alcohol-free day a week and a cap on any one night, with every drink logged.

standard.text: Two or more alcohol-free days, a cap of three on any one night, and a weekly limit, with every drink logged.

full.text: Three or more alcohol-free days, a cap of three on any one night, and a weekly limit within national guidance, with every drink logged.

levels.light: A cap on every night, set before the first drink, with drinks logged.
levels.standard: A cap on every night, plus one alcohol-free night a week, with drinks logged.
levels.full: A cap on every night, two or more alcohol-free nights a week, and a weekly limit within national guidance.

levels.light: A cap on each night out, set before you arrive, with a water between drinks.
levels.standard: A cap on each night out, and one night out a month without drinking.
levels.full: A cap on each night out, every other night out alcohol-free, and a weekly limit within national guidance.

alcohol.ifThenExample: When I pour or open a drink, I log it before the first sip.

ifThenExamplesFor.text: When I arrive somewhere I'll be drinking, I set my number and tell one person.
When I pour the first drink of the night, I log it and remind myself of the cap.

fitNotes.text: The nightly version: first drink after dinner, not before; two, then the fridge closes. Alcohol-free days come once the cap holds.
The night-out version: a cap of three, a water with every drink, and an exit line ready before you arrive: "I'm out after this one." Stay till the end if you like; the count still holds.
At social events, start with a non-alcoholic drink, and have a water with every drink after.
When you log, jot what was going on (stress, boredom, company). Patterns show up fast.
Track the money you keep alongside the drinks you skip.

safety.text: If you drink most nights and have ever had shakes, sweats or anxiety when you stopped, let a doctor plan the cut-back; stopping suddenly can be dangerous. Otherwise, start with the cap.
If you drink most days, or have ever had shakes, sweats or anxiety when you stopped, let a doctor plan the cut-back. Otherwise, you're clear to start.

notFor.reason: You drink little or none, so this one isn't needed.

alcohol.evidence: In 69 trials (33,642 people), brief advice sessions from a clinician cut drinking by about 20 g a week at one year versus little or no advice (roughly a pint of beer), with moderate certainty, though results varied a lot. They barely changed the number of drinking days (0.13 fewer a week). Self-set alcohol-free days are less proven.

sources.cite: Kaner et al. 2018, Cochrane: brief alcohol interventions, 69 trials

nicotine.name: Quit nicotine with support
nicotine.promise: I'll quit, with the support that roughly doubles my odds, not on willpower alone.
nicotine.core: Quit smoking or vaping with stop-smoking medication plus support from a quitline, app or counselor.

light.text: Set a quit date within a month and call a quitline.

standard.text: Set a quit date within two weeks; start medication and a quitline or app.

full.text: Quit date this week, with medication and 4 to 8 support sessions.

nicotine.ifThenExample: When I wake on my quit date, I start the medication and make my first quitline call.

fitNotes.text: US quitlines are free (1-800-QUIT-NOW), and many insurers cover the medication.
Pick the date now, and put it after the hardest week coming up.

safety.text: A quick check with a doctor or pharmacist tells you which stop-smoking medication is safe for you.

notFor.reason: You're smoke- and vape-free, so this one isn't needed.

nicotine.evidence: In 52 trials (19,488 people), medication plus support raised quit rates at six months or more by about 70–100% over usual care, brief advice or lighter support (RR 1.83), with high-quality evidence. Effects were larger when people were recruited through healthcare settings.

sources.cite: Cochrane: combined medication and behavioural support for smoking cessation, 53 trials

nature.name: Time in nature
nature.promise: I'll get outside every week, because my head works better out there.
nature.core: Spend time in green or blue spaces each week (parks, woods, water, tree-lined streets), split any way you like.

light.text: 60 minutes a week to start.

standard.text: 120 minutes a week, any split.

full.text: 120 minutes or more a week, over 3 or more visits.

nature.ifThenExample: When I have a day off, I take my coffee to the park.

fitNotes.text: Flat, paved paths or seated time in a park both count.
Sitting in a garden or park counts.
Playground and backyard time counts.
Sitting outside together counts; a porch or garden is enough.
A park-district walk or nature group gives company without needing an invite.
Go in daylight, to busy parks, or with someone.
Drive to a park and walk from the lot.
Batch it on the day off; one long visit counts the same as several short ones.
Try the break closest to daylight.

nature.evidence: Mixed. A 2026 second-order meta-analysis of 30 reviews found large effects of nature programs on anxiety (SMD −0.83) and depression (−0.72), but most studies compared against doing nothing, and a 183-RCT network meta-analysis found nature programs didn't beat control conditions on well-being. Against an urban walk, 7 small forest-bathing trials (250 people) found better short-term mood but no clear effect on depression. 120+ minutes a week went with better health in 19,806 adults (correlational). B until the trials get better comparison groups.

sources.cite: Saeedy Robat et al. 2026, Nature Human Behaviour: nature-based interventions, second-order meta-analysis of 30 reviews
2025 network meta-analysis, Nature Human Behaviour: wellbeing interventions, 183 RCTs
White et al. 2019, Scientific Reports: 120 minutes a week in nature, n = 19,806
2025 meta-analysis of RCTs: forest bathing and mood, 7 trials

rehab.name: Follow the rehab plan
rehab.promise: I'll do the plan my clinician gave me, exactly, because that is what gets me back.
rehab.core: Do the exercises your physical therapist or surgeon prescribed, on the prescribed schedule. No plan yet? Your first step is asking for one.

light.text: Exactly as prescribed.

standard.text: Exactly as prescribed.

full.text: Exactly as prescribed.

rehab.ifThenExample: When I finish breakfast, I do my PT exercises.

fitNotes.text: If your PT is fine with it, split the routine across the day.

rehab.evidence: Not graded here: the evidence belongs to your clinician's plan. The app's job is consistency. Pinned first for anyone recovering from injury or surgery, or waiting for surgery (prehab).

reach.name: Reach-out message
reach.promise: I'm someone who reaches out first.
reach.core: Reach out to someone you haven't talked to in a while. One message counts.

light.text: One message every two weeks.

standard.text: One message a week.

full.text: Two messages a week, one of them a call.

reach.ifThenExample: When I sit down on a Sunday evening, I message one person before I open social media.

fitNotes.text: No close friend right now? That's common. Start with an easy yes: a former coworker, classmate or neighbor.
Stuck on what to say? Borrow this: "Saw something that reminded me of you. How are you doing?"
Different hours? A voice note works anytime.

reach.evidence: Across preregistered experiments with more than 5,900 people, recipients appreciated being contacted more than senders expected, most of all from weak ties. The trials measured appreciation, not the sender's own wellbeing.

sources.cite: Liu et al. 2022, JPSP: the surprise of reaching out

lonely.name: Test lonely thoughts
lonely.promise: I'll catch the thoughts that keep me on my own, and put them to the test.
lonely.core: When a thought like "no one wants to hear from me" shows up, write it down and check it against the evidence before you act on it.

light.text: Log one thought a week and write one piece of counter-evidence.

standard.text: Log thoughts as they come and test each one against the evidence.

full.text: Log and test each thought, then act on one: send the message the thought said not to send.

lonely.ifThenExample: When I catch myself thinking no one cares, I open my thought log.

fitNotes.text: A voice memo works instead of writing.
Pair it with a set weekly call so the test has somewhere to go.

lonely.evidence: In a 2025 meta-analysis of 16 RCTs (2,476 people) against waitlist or no-treatment controls, loneliness interventions helped post-treatment (g = 0.65), with CBT the most effective (g = 0.73); but effects varied widely, shrank to non-significant after correcting for publication bias, and weren't significant at follow-up. An earlier analysis of 20 randomized trials found a small overall effect, largest for programs targeting unhelpful thoughts about others. Trials were mostly professionally led, so the self-guided version is graded B.

sources.cite: Zeas-Sigüenza et al. 2025: loneliness interventions, 25 studies (16 RCTs pooled)
Masi et al. 2011: meta-analysis of interventions to reduce loneliness

group.name: Join a recurring group
group.promise: I'll have somewhere I'm expected, on a schedule I keep.
group.core: Pick one recurring group (a club, class, team, faith or volunteer group) and hold its sessions like fixed appointments.

light.text: One group session a month.

standard.text: One group session a week.

full.text: One group session a week, plus one extra contact with a member between sessions.

group.ifThenExample: When I have group night, I leave home 10 minutes early.

fitNotes.text: Pick a seated or low-effort group: a book club, choir, craft or discussion group.
Library, park-district, faith and volunteer groups are free.
Pick one within a 20-minute drive, so it still works in busy weeks.
Changing shifts? An online or drop-in group fits.
Try a parents' group, or one with childcare.
A caregiver support group counts, and many meet online or by phone.

group.evidence: In an RCT of 174 lonely, depressed young people (15–25), a program built on group membership matched dose-matched group CBT for depression at 12 months and showed a slight edge for loneliness that emerged after treatment ended, though the 12-month difference was not clear-cut. One program, one unblinded trial, promising.

sources.cite: Groups 4 Health vs CBT, randomised trial with 12-month follow-up

thanks.name: Thank someone specific
thanks.promise: I'll tell people what they did for me, specifically.
thanks.core: Tell one person something specific they did that helped you. One sentence counts.

light.text: One thank-you sentence, every two weeks.

standard.text: One specific thank-you note a week.

full.text: One specific note a week, plus one longer letter a month.

thanks.ifThenExample: When I sit down to lunch on a Friday, I send one thank-you message.

fitNotes.text: A service worker, teacher, neighbor or online creator all count.

notFor.reason: You've had low mood most days, and gratitude exercises can feel invalidating then. Sleep, movement, activity scheduling or a reach-out come first.

thanks.evidence: In 23 RCTs (6,745 people), expressing gratitude to a person improved wellbeing versus neutral activities (g = 0.22), but not clearly versus other active exercises (g = 0.12). The largest analysis, 163 samples and 24,804 people in 28 countries, put the overall gratitude effect at g = 0.19 and expressing it specifically at 0.15, no better than other positive activities (few comparisons). Plenty of trials, small benefit.

sources.cite: Choi et al. 2025, PNAS: gratitude interventions across 28 countries, 163 samples, n = 24,804
Kirca et al. 2023: expressed gratitude, 25 RCTs
Cregg & Cheavens 2021, J. Happiness Studies: gratitude and depression/anxiety

lovekind.name: Loving-kindness minutes
lovekind.promise: I'll practice wishing people well, starting with me.
lovekind.core: Sit for a few minutes and silently wish yourself well, then a friend, a neutral person, then a wider circle.

light.text: 3 minutes, three times a week.

standard.text: 10 minutes a day.

full.text: 15 minutes a day, plus one silent good wish for a stranger during the day.

lovekind.ifThenExample: When I finish brushing my teeth at night, I do my loving-kindness minutes.

fitNotes.text: Free recordings work fine; no subscription needed.
Include someone you used to be close to; it tends to make a reach-out feel easier.
Skip the difficult-person stage. You and a friend are enough.
Add the person you're in conflict with last, and only when it feels possible.
Try it while the kids fall asleep, or in the car before going in.
Try it in the car before going in, or beside them while they rest.

lovekind.evidence: A 2024 meta-analysis of 23 RCTs found loving-kindness practice raised positive affect (g = 0.44), lowered negative affect (g = 0.44) and raised compassion (g = 0.36) against no-treatment controls, but each estimate rests on only 3 small trials with self-reported outcomes and high measurement bias. It worked the same with or without a live teacher. Against active controls it showed no clear benefit, and other practices did slightly better at reducing negative feelings.

sources.cite: Petrovic et al. 2024, Clinical Psychology Review: loving-kindness interventions, 23 RCTs, n ≈ 3,300

kind.name: Small kind acts
kind.promise: I'll do kind things on purpose, including for myself.
kind.core: Do one small, deliberate kind act, rotating who it's for. You count too.

light.text: Three kind acts a week.

standard.text: One kind act a day.

full.text: One kind act a day, plus one bigger act on the weekend.

kind.ifThenExample: When I sit down at my desk, I pick today's kind act.

fitNotes.text: Free acts count: a specific compliment, holding a place, sharing something useful.
Spending on someone else counts as an act.
Most days, let the act be one for yourself.
Strangers and online communities count.

kind.evidence: In 27 experimental studies (4,045 people, mostly students), kindness raised wellbeing by a small-to-medium amount (d = 0.28), roughly 0.6 points on a 10-point scale. Most studies were small and measured only short-term effects. In one 7-day experiment (683 adults), kindness to close ties, strangers or oneself worked about equally well, though its no-kindness comparison group wasn't randomized.

sources.cite: Curry et al. 2018, JESP: kindness meta-analysis
Rowland & Curry 2019, J. Social Psychology: kindness to different recipients, n = 683

checkin.name: Partner check-in
checkin.promise: I'll make time, on a schedule, to really talk with my partner.
checkin.core: On a set day, sit down with your partner and cover what went well, one thing to work on, and one appreciation.

light.text: A 10-minute check-in, every other week.

standard.text: A 15-minute check-in, weekly.

full.text: A 15-minute check-in weekly, plus a longer quarterly review of the relationship.

checkin.ifThenExample: When we finish dinner on a check-in Sunday, I start our check-in before any screens.

fitNotes.text: Book it like a meeting on the one day you're both off.
Try it after the kids are asleep, or on a walk together.

safety.text: If you ever feel afraid of your partner, this isn't the right tool. The app shows you support resources first.

notFor.reason: You're not in a relationship, so this one isn't needed.

checkin.evidence: In an RCT of 215 couples, a structured relationship check-up raised intimacy across 2 years (mean d = 0.37) and satisfaction for most of that time. That check-up was run by trained clinicians once a year; the self-run weekly version borrows the format and has not been trialed on its own.

sources.cite: Cordova et al. 2014: Marriage Checkup RCT, 215 couples

conflict.name: Cool-down, then I-statements
conflict.promise: I'll cool down before I speak, and then say what I feel.
conflict.core: When a disagreement heats up, take a 20-minute break, then come back and speak in "I feel ___ when ___" statements.

light.text: Take the break; add I-statements once you're calm enough.

standard.text: The break and I-statements, in every heated disagreement.

full.text: Break and I-statements, plus a short repair message after each disagreement.

conflict.ifThenExample: When I notice my voice rising, I say "I need 20 minutes" and step away.

fitNotes.text: At work, the break can sound like "let me think about this and come back after lunch."
During the break, try grounding: name 5 things you see, 4 you hear.

safety.text: If you ever feel afraid of the person you're in conflict with, communication skills come second. The app shows you support resources first.

conflict.evidence: Across 117 studies (37 experiments on communication), relationship-education programs improved communication skills (d = 0.44 in experiments), mostly in White, middle-class married couples, and follow-up gains came mainly from published studies. The programs teach these skills as a package, not this habit alone.

sources.cite: Hawkins et al. 2008: relationship education meta-analysis, 117 studies

goodnews.name: Celebrate good news
goodnews.promise: When someone I love has good news, I'll make it a moment.
goodnews.core: When someone shares good news, respond with interest and questions before you change the subject.

light.text: Once a day, with one person.

standard.text: Every time someone close shares good news.

full.text: Every time, plus a follow-up later ("How did the new job's first week go?").

goodnews.ifThenExample: When I hear someone's good news, I ask one follow-up question first.

fitNotes.text: Start with your partner at dinner.

goodnews.evidence: Responding enthusiastically to others' good news is linked to relationship quality in correlational and diary studies. There's no strong intervention trial.

sources.cite: Gable et al. 2004, JPSP: responses to shared good news

forgive.name: Work through a grudge
forgive.promise: I'll work through the grudge, so it stops costing me.
forgive.core: Work through one grudge with the REACH steps across several sessions: recall the hurt, empathize, offer forgiveness as a gift, commit to it, hold on to it.

light.text: 10 minutes, every other week, starting with a small, old grudge.

standard.text: 20 minutes, weekly.

full.text: 30 minutes, weekly.

forgive.ifThenExample: When I finish dinner on a Sunday, I open the forgiveness worksheet.

fitNotes.text: Aim for emotional forgiveness; it doesn't require trusting or reconciling with the person.

notFor.reason: Your conflict is with someone you live with, so this waits. Safety and support come first, and the app shows support resources instead.
Your mood has been low, so this waits until it's steadier.

forgive.evidence: Across 54 reports (2,323 people at post-treatment), explicit forgiveness programs raised forgiveness well above no treatment (Δ = 0.56) and above other therapies (Δ = 0.45), with gains holding at follow-up; longer programs worked better. Results varied a lot between studies (I² about 72–77%), and not all studies were randomized.

sources.cite: Wade et al. 2014, JCCP: forgiveness interventions meta-analysis

buffer.name: Ask clearly, say no
buffer.promise: I'll ask for what I need and say no when I mean it.
buffer.core: State a need or turn down a request, clearly and respectfully. Start with low-stakes situations.

light.text: One low-stakes practice a week: return an item, ask a question, decline an upsell.

standard.text: One assertive ask or no a week, using "I" statements.

full.text: Two or three asks or no's a week, including one that feels harder.

levels.light: One small no a week: an optional meeting, an extra errand, a favor that isn't yours to do.
levels.standard: One clear no or ask a week that gives you back an hour, using "I" statements.
levels.full: Two or three a week, including one that feels harder, and one standing block you protect.

buffer.ifThenExample: When I get an optional ask, I pause and decide before I answer.

fitNotes.text: Not sure? Buy time first: "Let me check and get back to you tomorrow."
Use it for optional asks from outside the household, not care duties.
Use it for extra projects and meetings, not core duties.

buffer.evidence: In 12 RCTs (503 people), assertiveness training reduced social anxiety (g = 0.62) with moderate certainty, compared with no treatment or placebo rather than another therapy. Only 3 trials checked whether gains lasted. Trials were structured programs, in person or online, not self-practice, so this habit is graded B.

sources.cite: 2026 meta-analysis of 12 RCTs: assertiveness training for social anxiety

breathe.name: Slow breathing
breathe.promise: I'll slow my breathing and bring the rest of me down with it.
breathe.core: Breathe slowly for a few minutes, about six breaths a minute, with the out-breath longer than the in-breath.

light.text: 2 minutes, once a day.

standard.text: 5 minutes, once a day.

full.text: 5 minutes twice a day, plus one minute whenever stress spikes.

breathe.ifThenExample: When I sit down in the car before driving home, I do my slow breathing.

fitNotes.text: Use it in the moment: one minute before a hard conversation or after a hard call.
Make it the first step of your wind-down after a shift.
No privacy needed: do it while waiting on someone or while the kettle boils.
A free timer or a paced-breathing video is all it takes.

safety.text: Keep the pace comfortable, and stop if you feel lightheaded.

breathe.evidence: In 12 RCTs (785 people), breathing practice lowered stress (g = −0.35); in larger sets it lowered anxiety (g = −0.32) and depression (g = −0.40). The benefit came from slow-paced breathing; fast breathing was tested in only two trials and showed no effect. Small trials, some with risk of bias, and more practice did not mean bigger effects.

sources.cite: Fincham et al. 2023, Scientific Reports: breathwork and stress, 12 RCTs, n = 785

nameit.name: Mindful awareness
nameit.promise: I'll notice what I feel without having to fix it.
nameit.core: Notice what's happening right now, feelings included, without judging or fixing it.

light.text: Once a day, name a strong feeling in a few words and pause for 60 seconds.

standard.text: 10 minutes of guided practice a day.

full.text: 20 minutes a day, plus naming feelings in the moment.

nameit.ifThenExample: When I wake up, I sit for my practice before I look at my phone.

ifThenExamplesFor.text: When I get the kids down for the night, I sit for my practice.
When I arrive at work, I sit for my practice before going in.

fitNotes.text: Feeling flooded? Ground first (5 things seen, 4 heard, 3 touched), then name the feeling.
No privacy? Practice silently in the car or shower.
Free recorded practices work; no paid app needed.
A group class adds company, and it matches how the trials were run.
Some employers and health plans cover a mindfulness program or app. One email can tell you.

nameit.evidence: In a network meta-analysis of 183 RCTs (22,811 adults), mindfulness improved wellbeing versus no-treatment or waitlist controls (SMD 0.44), though 60% of trials had a high risk of bias. A separate analysis of 13 RCTs (2,371 adults) found teacher-led group programs cut distress for 1–6 months (SMD −0.32) versus no program, but not versus other active programs. Two umbrella reviews of workplace programs found mindfulness had the most consistent effects on stress, though most evidence was low certainty. Observational studies link accepting rather than judging negative feelings to better mental health months later.

sources.cite: 2025 network meta-analysis, Nature Human Behaviour: wellbeing interventions, 183 RCTs
2023 IPD meta-analysis, Nature Mental Health: mindfulness programs, 13 RCTs
Ford et al. 2018, JPSP: accepting negative emotions
Virtanen et al. 2025, Lancet Public Health: workplace health promotion, 88 meta-analyses
Miguel et al. 2023, Occup Environ Med: WHO umbrella review of workplace mental health interventions, 16 meta-analyses

selfcomp.name: Self-compassion break
selfcomp.promise: I'll talk to myself the way I'd talk to a friend.
selfcomp.core: When you slip or struggle, treat yourself as you would a friend: name that it's hard, remember others struggle too, and offer a kind word.

light.text: Once a day, at the hardest moment.

standard.text: Whenever self-criticism shows up.

full.text: In the moment, plus a 5-minute self-compassion letter each week.

selfcomp.ifThenExample: When I catch myself thinking "I'm so stupid", I put a hand on my chest and say what I'd tell a friend.

fitNotes.text: Three phrases are enough: "This is hard. Others feel this too. May I be kind to myself."
Try it after every rejection or no-reply.

selfcomp.evidence: In 27 RCTs (1,480 people, mostly vs waitlist), self-compassion interventions reduced depression (g = 0.66; 0.79 against active controls), stress (g = 0.67) and self-criticism (g = 0.56); rumination fell sharply (g = 1.37) but in only 4 trials. A 183-RCT network meta-analysis found compassion-based programs improved wellbeing moderately (SMD about 0.41), about as much as mindfulness or exercise, though 60% of its trials were at high risk of bias. Only 1 of the 27 trials was preregistered.

sources.cite: Ferrari et al. 2019, Mindfulness: self-compassion interventions, 27 RCTs
2025 network meta-analysis, Nature Human Behaviour: wellbeing interventions, 183 RCTs

activate.name: Schedule what matters
activate.promise: I'll put what matters on my calendar, and do it whatever my mood.
activate.core: Schedule activities that bring enjoyment, a sense of accomplishment, or live out a value you named, then do them whatever your mood.

light.text: One small scheduled activity every other day.

standard.text: One scheduled activity a day.

full.text: One activity a day, plus a weekly look at which lifted your mood most.

activate.ifThenExample: When I plan tomorrow each evening, I put one enjoyable or meaningful activity on the calendar.

fitNotes.text: Free activities count: a walk, a library book, a call, a hobby you already have.
Ten-minute activities count.
Start smaller than seems worth it. Action tends to come before motivation.

activate.evidence: In 26 RCTs (1,524 people), behavioral activation reduced depression by a large amount (SMD −0.74), and the effect held moderately at 6–9 months. Most trials were small and of low quality.

sources.cite: Ekers et al. 2014, PLOS One: behavioural activation, 26 RCTs

block.name: Protected focus block
block.promise: I'll protect one block a week for the thing that matters most to me.
block.core: Reserve one fixed, phone-away block each week for the goal that matters most. Treat it like an appointment you keep.

light.text: One 25-minute block a week.

standard.text: Three 25-minute blocks a week, on the same days.

full.text: Five blocks a week, plus a weekly note of what moved.

levels.light: One protected 90-minute block a week, on the calendar, phone away.
levels.standard: One meeting-free half-day a week, on the calendar.
levels.full: One meeting-free half-day a week, plus one evening fully off.

block.ifThenExample: When I finish breakfast on a block day, I put my phone in the drawer and open the one thing.

ifThenExamplesFor.text: When I reach naptime or bedtime, I put my phone in the drawer and open the one thing.
When I finish breakfast on my day off, I open the one thing.

fitNotes.text: Shorter than feels right works: 25 minutes during a nap beats 90 that stay a plan.
Try before work, not after; evenings tend to get eaten.
If roommates make home impossible, head out: a library or café table is your office.

block.evidence: Time-management practices go with better wellbeing (r ≈ .31) and performance (r ≈ .26) across 158 studies (53,957 people), but most of those studies are cross-sectional and the trials are few and weak, so this is a practical tactic that borrows its power from the if-then cue and from protecting the time before other demands take it.

sources.cite: Aeon et al. 2021, PLOS One: does time management work? 158 studies
Young et al. 2026, Applied Psychology: Health and Well-Being: time-management interventions, 7 trials, n = 442

ifthen.name: If-then planning
ifthen.promise: I'll decide in advance, so the moment doesn't decide for me.
ifthen.core: Write plans in the form "If [situation], then I will [action]" for your current goal.

light.text: One plan a week, for the easiest step.

standard.text: One plan a week.

full.text: Two or three plans a week, including one for the likeliest obstacle.

ifthen.ifThenExample: When I sit down at the start of my week, I write one if-then for the goal.

ifThenExamplesFor.text: When I get next week's schedule, I write the if-then for it.

fitNotes.text: Tie the "if" to an event, not a clock time: "If I get home from a shift…"

ifthen.evidence: Across 94 tests with more than 8,000 people, if-then plans improved goal attainment over intention alone by a medium-to-large amount (d = 0.65).

sources.cite: Gollwitzer & Sheeran 2006: implementation intentions, 94 tests

monitor.name: Track and share progress
monitor.promise: I'll track my progress and let someone see it.
monitor.core: On a set day each week, write down your progress toward the goal and share it with someone.

light.text: Record your progress weekly and send one line about it to one person.

standard.text: Record weekly and walk one person through it.

full.text: Record daily and share weekly.

monitor.ifThenExample: When I wrap up on Friday afternoon, I write down the week's progress and share it with one person.

ifThenExamplesFor.text: When I get my next schedule, I write down last week's progress and share it with one person.

fitNotes.text: No one close to share with? An online group or a coach works.

monitor.evidence: In 138 randomized studies (19,951 people), prompting progress monitoring improved goal attainment (d = 0.40), and more so when progress was physically recorded or reported to others. Almost all involved health goals such as weight, activity and blood pressure.

sources.cite: Harkin et al. 2016, Psychological Bulletin: monitoring goal progress, 138 studies

practice.name: Deliberate skill practice
practice.promise: I'll get good at this the way anyone does: short, focused, often.
practice.core: Practice a skill you choose in short, spaced sessions, testing yourself instead of re-reading.

light.text: Two 15-minute sessions a week.

standard.text: 20 minutes, 4 days a week.

full.text: 30 minutes most days, plus one test of the full skill each week.

practice.ifThenExample: When I get home from work on a practice day, I do my practice block.

fitNotes.text: Library courses and free online classes count.
Use commutes or lunch for 10-minute recall drills.
Pick the skill your target role asks for most.
Use it for your course or credential: quiz yourself on this week's material instead of rereading it.

practice.evidence: A large meta-analysis found practice testing beat re-studying across ages, materials and settings, and spacing sessions over time adds to it.

sources.cite: Adesope et al. 2017, Review of Educational Research: practice testing meta-analysis

savor.name: Stretch the good moment
savor.promise: I'll slow down for the good moments instead of rushing past them.
savor.core: When something good happens, pause to notice it, then share it or write it down.

light.text: Once a day, pause on one good moment.

standard.text: 30 seconds, whenever something good happens.

full.text: Whenever something good happens, plus sharing one moment with someone daily.

savor.ifThenExample: When I laugh or relax, I pause and notice what's good about it.

fitNotes.text: Share one good moment with your partner at dinner.
Do it in the moment or on paper, not only with a tap in the app; that's the form the trials tested.
Savoring a memory counts; older adults did well in the trials.

notFor.reason: Your stress is high, and calming comes before savoring. Calming habits come first for now.

savor.evidence: In 20 RCTs (4,805 people), savoring practice improved emotional wellbeing by a medium amount (g = 0.51), and the effect held against active comparison activities (g = 0.30) with no sign of publication bias. Most trials ran about two weeks. Guided or written exercises carried the result; the few app-only trials were too small to be sure.

sources.cite: Chen et al. 2026, Applied Psychology: Health and Well-Being: savoring interventions, 20 RCTs, n = 4,805

search.name: Job-search block
search.promise: I'll run my search like a job: a set block each time, then I clock out.
search.core: Work a set search block that ends with a plan for the next one, and stay in touch with people in the field you want.

light.text: Search 25 minutes, 3 days a week; reach one contact every two weeks.

standard.text: Search 45 minutes on weekdays; reach one contact a week.

ownerblock.name: Weekly business block
ownerblock.promise: I'll work on my business once a week, not just in it.
ownerblock.core: Once a week, set aside a block for the business itself rather than client work: records and invoices, prices, and one step toward growth, such as a hiring call, a quote follow-up or asking a happy customer for a referral.

light.text: One 45-minute block a week: invoices and records first, then one growth step.

standard.text: One 60-minute block a week, with one growth step every week.

full.text: One 90-minute block a week, plus a monthly look at prices and numbers.

fitNotes.text: Busy season? Keep the block but shrink it to the invoices; the growth step can wait a week.
Chase what you're owed first; unpaid invoices are the cheapest money you'll ever find.
A fixed block protects family time too: business admin stops leaking into evenings.

ownerblock.evidence: Across more than 20,000 small firms in seven countries, basic practices like record-keeping, pricing and marketing predicted higher sales, profits and survival. That link is correlational. In trials, training raised these practices only modestly; pooled across trials it raised profits about 10% and sales about 5%, too small for most single trials to detect.

sources.cite: McKenzie & Woodruff 2017, Management Science: business practices in small firms in seven countries
McKenzie 2021, Oxford Review of Economic Policy: small business training meta-analysis, profits and sales up 5–10% on average

certstudy.name: Certification study block
certstudy.promise: I'll work toward my certificate in short sessions that test me.
certstudy.core: Study for one named exam or certificate in short, spaced sessions: one section per session, and close each one with practice questions instead of re-reading.

light.text: Two 25-minute sessions a week, one exam section each.

standard.text: Three 25-minute sessions a week, with a practice test every other week.

full.text: Four 30-minute sessions a week, plus a full timed practice test each week.

In separate, mostly one-time surveys of 91 samples (38,124 employees), detachment went with less exhaustion (r = −0.36) and higher life satisfaction (r = 0.32). The studies were of employees and training programs, not business owners or this exact step.

fitNotes.text: Growing something you give to? Each block is one step: brief or recruit one helper, plan one session, or call one partner.
Stuck? Start each block by writing the very next physical step, even if it's only getting the materials out. Stalls end with small starts.
Making something? Work on the piece itself, not on planning it. A rough 25 minutes beats a perfect plan.
Building something? Each block ends with the next step written down and, once a month, one conversation with someone you'd serve.
Moving up? Make each block one visible step: a piece of the bigger role done early, a problem solved and written up, or a conversation with the person who decides.

Try before work, not after; evenings tend to get eaten.
A full week? Keep the block, shrink it to 15 minutes. Showing up is the habit.

full.text: Once a week, 15 minutes: compare spending by category to a monthly plan, and check the next 30 days.

In 76 randomized financial-education experiments, money behavior improved slightly (0.10 SD), especially saving and budgeting, but none tested a weekly check-in. Indirect evidence only.

Kaiser et al. 2022, Journal of Financial Economics: financial education, 76 RCTs

debtpay.evidence: In data on nearly 6,000 clients of one debt-settlement firm, those who had more individual accounts closed out were more likely to eliminate their debt overall.
