full.text: Set a deposit limit, turn every urge into a savings transfer, and tally what the swap saved each week.

betswap.ifThenExample: When I open a betting app, I close it and move the stake to savings.

fitNotes.text: Set the limit at what you could lose without it mattering. If that number is zero, the limit is zero.
Tell your partner the limit; a limit someone else knows tends to hold.

safety.text: If you're hiding bets or chasing losses, start with a gambling helpline, before any habit: {GAMBLING_LINE}.

notFor.reason: You're not putting money on bets, so this one isn't needed.

betswap.evidence: Deposit limits and pre-commitment reduce spending among people who set them in operator data and small trials; the stake-to-savings swap is a practical tactic without trial data of its own.

fundamentals.name: Learn money basics
fundamentals.promise: I'll learn how money works, one short lesson at a time.
fundamentals.core: Learn one money topic at a time (budgeting, interest, debt, retirement) and put one thing from each to use.

light.text: Do one 10-minute lesson every two weeks.

standard.text: Do one 15-minute lesson a week.

full.text: Do one lesson a week, and act on one thing from it the same week.

fundamentals.ifThenExample: When I sit down with coffee on a Saturday morning, I do my money lesson.

fitNotes.text: Free courses from a public library, a bank or a government consumer site all count.

fundamentals.evidence: A meta-analysis of 76 randomized experiments with more than 160,000 people found financial education improved financial knowledge (0.20 SD) and financial behavior (0.10 SD), most reliably saving and budgeting. The effects are small, vary a lot between programs, and fade somewhat after six months.

sources.cite: Kaiser et al. 2022, Journal of Financial Economics: financial education, 76 RCTs

buytime.name: Buy back your time
buytime.promise: I'll buy back my time where it's cheapest to buy.
buytime.core: Each month, hand off one chore you dislike: pay for it or trade it.

light.text: Hand off one small thing a month.

standard.text: Hand off one chore a month.

full.text: Hand off two chores a month.

buytime.ifThenExample: When I turn the calendar to a new month, I pick one chore to hand off.

fitNotes.text: Skip paying: trade chores with a friend or neighbor.
Pay for it: a cleaner, laundry service or grocery delivery.
Swap one block of childcare or errands with another parent.
Respite care, a paid sitter or a relative taking one block a week buys you the most time.
Renegotiate one recurring chore with your partner.

buytime.evidence: Across 6,271 adults in four countries, spending on time-saving services went with higher life satisfaction. The causal test was a 60-person study: on the day people spent $40 on a time-saving purchase instead of a material one, they reported better mood and less time pressure.

sources.cite: Whillans et al. 2017, PNAS: buying time promotes happiness

story.name: What mattered this week
story.promise: I'll write down what mattered this week, and to whom.
story.core: Write about something you did that mattered, and to whom. Three sentences count.

light.text: Three sentences a week.

standard.text: 10 minutes a week.

full.text: 20 minutes a week, plus rereading last month's entries.

story.ifThenExample: When I get ready for bed on a Sunday night, I write what mattered this week, and to whom.

fitNotes.text: Try writing about a past chapter of life and what it gave others.
Care you gave counts. Name who it helped.

story.evidence: In a meta-analysis of 33 RCTs (2,895 people), programs raised meaning in life (SMD 0.62). Narrative approaches, such as reflective writing, held up against active controls (SMD 0.61 across 6 trials). Most trials were small and in people facing illness.

sources.cite: Manco & Hamby 2021, AJHP: meaning-in-life interventions, 33 RCTs, n = 2,895

bps.name: Best possible self
bps.promise: I'll write the best realistic version of my future, and take one step toward it.
bps.core: Write about your life going as well as it realistically could in the future, then name one step toward it.

light.text: 10 minutes, once a month.

standard.text: 15 minutes, every two weeks.

full.text: 15 minutes a week for a month, then monthly.

bps.ifThenExample: When I sit down on the first Sunday of the month, I write my best possible self.

fitNotes.text: Pick one area of life, not all of them.

bps.evidence: In 29 studies (2,909 people), the best-possible-self exercise raised positive affect (d = 0.51), optimism (d = 0.33) and wellbeing (d = 0.33); effects on depression were small (d = 0.12).

sources.cite: Carrillo et al. 2019, PLOS One: best possible self meta-analysis

volunteer.name: Volunteer on a schedule
volunteer.promise: I'll give my time to something that needs it, on a schedule I keep.
volunteer.core: Give time to a cause on a regular schedule you can keep.

light.text: Volunteer once a month.

standard.text: Volunteer every other week.

full.text: Volunteer weekly.

levels.light: This month: find one place and book a first slot (one call or visit). Then once a month.
levels.standard: This week: contact one place and book a first slot. Then every other week.
levels.full: This week: contact one place and book a first slot. Then weekly.

volunteer.ifThenExample: When I sit down to plan my week, I put my next volunteer slot on the calendar.

ifThenExamplesFor.text: When I get my schedule for the month, I book one volunteer slot on a day off.
When I sit down to plan my week, I take one step toward a first slot: one call or email, or booking the date.

fitNotes.text: It costs time, not money; pick something close by.
Pick flexible or remote volunteering: crisis-text lines, tutoring online, one-off events.
An in-person role with a regular team doubles as a group.
Pick a seated role: phone, admin, mentoring.

notFor.reason: You've had low mood most days, and a new commitment to others can drain you further. Writing about what already mattered, and activity scheduling, come first.
You're already giving care under heavy stress, so more giving can wait until that eases. What you already do counts as mattering.

volunteer.evidence: In a review of 40 papers, volunteers in cohort studies had about 20% lower mortality and less depression, but the experimental trials haven't confirmed the mental-health benefits. In a 2021 meta-analysis of meaning-in-life trials, prosocial programs showed no significant effect (2 small trials). B rests on the long-term cohort data.

sources.cite: Jenkinson et al. 2013, BMC Public Health: volunteering systematic review
Manco & Hamby 2021, AJHP: meaning-in-life interventions, 33 RCTs, n = 2,895

expressive.name: Write it out
expressive.promise: I'll write out what's heavy, so it weighs less.
expressive.core: Write freely about a current stress or hard experience, including your feelings and what it means to you.

light.text: 10 minutes, once a week.

standard.text: 15 minutes, once a week for four weeks.

full.text: 20 minutes, once a week, then a monthly session.

expressive.ifThenExample: When I sit down on a Wednesday evening, I write about what's weighing on me.

fitNotes.text: Use a private notes app or a locked journal.
Keep it on a locked device, not paper at home.

safety.text: If writing brings up overwhelming distress, stop and talk to someone. With trauma, do this with a therapist, so you have support.

expressive.evidence: Across 146 randomized studies, writing about difficult experiences improved psychological and physical health by a small but statistically significant amount (r = .075); it did not change health behaviors. Weekly sessions tended to beat daily ones, and being assigned current stresses helped mental health more than choosing between current and past ones.

sources.cite: Frattaroli 2006, Psychological Bulletin: experimental disclosure, 146 studies

socialmedia.name: Social media cap
socialmedia.promise: I'll cap the scroll and take my attention back.
socialmedia.core: Cap your daily time on social media apps, using your phone's built-in limits.

light.text: An hour a day in total.

standard.text: About 30 minutes a day in total (10 per app).

full.text: 30 minutes a day, and none in the first and last hour of the day.

socialmedia.ifThenExample: When I see the app limit pop up, I close the app and stand up.

fitNotes.text: Keep messaging real friends: cap the feeds, not the chats.
Job searching on LinkedIn counts as search time, not feed time.

socialmedia.evidence: In an RCT of 143 students, limiting Facebook, Instagram and Snapchat to 10 minutes each a day for 3 weeks reduced loneliness versus normal use, and cut depression only among those who started out more depressed. One short trial at one university, with no lasting follow-up.

sources.cite: Hunt et al. 2018, JSCP: limiting social media, RCT of 143 students

reading.name: Read fiction
reading.promise: I'll read fiction and let my mind go somewhere else for a while.
reading.core: Read fiction on a regular schedule. Ten minutes counts.

light.text: 10 minutes, three times a week.

standard.text: 20 minutes a day.

full.text: 30 minutes a day.

reading.ifThenExample: When I get into bed, I read before I sleep.

fitNotes.text: Try library books and the library's free e-book app.
Audiobooks on the commute count.
A library book club doubles as a group.

reading.evidence: A meta-analysis of 14 experiments found fiction reading produced a small improvement in social cognition, the ability to understand others' thoughts and feelings (g ≈ 0.15), versus non-fiction or no reading.

sources.cite: Dodell-Feder & Tamir 2018, JEP: General: fiction reading and social cognition, 14 studies

explore.name: Explore career options
explore.promise: I'll find out what's actually out there before I decide.
explore.core: Explore one career option at a time. Read about it, talk to someone in it, or try a small piece of the work; any of these counts.

light.text: Explore one option a month.

standard.text: Explore one option every two weeks, including one conversation.

full.text: Explore one option a week, with one conversation or a small trial project.

explore.ifThenExample: When I wake up on a Saturday, I spend time on this month's career option.

fitNotes.text: Free career services at libraries, workforce centers or alumni offices add counselor support, which raised effects.
Start by reading, then have one easy conversation with a former coworker.

explore.evidence: Across 57 studies (7,364 people, about half college students), career choice interventions improved outcomes versus no treatment or waitlist (d = 0.35), most for confidence in making career decisions. Outcomes were self-reported, not actual career results. Counselor support and written exercises seemed to raise the effect, though the authors call this tentative.

sources.cite: Whiston et al. 2017, JVB: career choice interventions, 57 studies

strengths.name: Use a strength at work
strengths.promise: I'll use what I'm good at, on purpose.
strengths.core: Put one of your top strengths to work in a new way, on a regular schedule.

light.text: Use a strength in a new way once every two weeks.

standard.text: Use a strength in a new way once a week.

full.text: Use a strength in a new way once a week, plus a monthly talk with your manager about using it more.

strengths.ifThenExample: When I start work on a Monday morning, I pick where to use my strength next.

fitNotes.text: Long hours? Swap an existing task for one that uses your strength, instead of adding work.

notFor.reason: You're not in a job right now, so this one can wait.

strengths.evidence: In two small online studies of employees (148 and 82 people), strengths exercises didn't beat control groups on job performance or engagement. People whose strengths use actually rose reported gains, but that was an after-the-fact comparison of 22 people. Evidence is from small studies with heavy dropout and self-rated outcomes.

sources.cite: 2023, Current Psychology: employee strengths interventions

timeblock.name: Plan the day's top three
timeblock.promise: I'll name what matters before the day names it for me.
timeblock.core: Pick the day's three most important tasks and block time for them before anything else.

light.text: Pick one top task a day and block time for it.

standard.text: Pick three top tasks a day and block time for the first.

full.text: Pick three top tasks a day, block time for all three, and review what got done each week.

timeblock.ifThenExample: When I reach for my email, I write my top three and block time for the first.

fitNotes.text: Shifts vary? Plan at the start of each shift, not each calendar day.
It works for search, study or household projects too.

timeblock.evidence: Across 158 studies (53,957 people), time management went with better performance (r ≈ .26) and more strongly with wellbeing (r ≈ .31), plus somewhat lower distress (r ≈ −.22). Mostly correlational. A 2026 systematic review found only 7 trials (442 people), all low quality, with inconsistent results.

sources.cite: Aeon et al. 2021, PLOS One: does time management work? 158 studies
Young et al. 2026, Applied Psychology: Health and Well-Being: time-management interventions, 7 trials, n = 442

feedback.name: Ask for feedback
feedback.promise: I'll ask one specific question about my work, and listen to the answer.
feedback.core: Ask a manager, peer or client for specific feedback on one piece of work. One question counts.

light.text: Ask for feedback once a month.

standard.text: Ask for feedback every two weeks.

full.text: Ask for feedback weekly, and act on one piece of it each time.

feedback.ifThenExample: When I finish a deliverable, I ask one person one specific question about it.

fitNotes.text: Try "What's one thing that would make this better?" It's easier to hear than open criticism.
No manager to ask? After a job, ask a customer or crew member one specific question.

notFor.reason: You're not in a job right now, so this one can wait.

feedback.evidence: In a meta-analysis of workplace studies, feedback seeking was linked to performance, but the link was small and the data correlational.

sources.cite: Anseel et al. 2015, Journal of Management: feedback-seeking meta-analysis

mentor.name: Meet a mentor
mentor.promise: I'll learn from someone further down the road than me.
mentor.core: Meet regularly with someone further along in your field for guidance.

light.text: Meet once a quarter.

standard.text: Meet once a month.

full.text: Meet every two weeks, with one agreed action between meetings.

mentor.ifThenExample: When I get to the first Thursday of the month, I have coffee with my mentor.

fitNotes.text: A formal mentoring program through a professional association or alumni network takes the awkward ask off your plate.
Look for another owner a few years ahead; free small-business mentoring programs can pair you.
A 30-minute video call counts.

mentor.evidence: A multidisciplinary meta-analysis of 112 studies found mentored people had slightly better career, attitudinal and health outcomes than non-mentored people; effects were small, larger for academic and workplace than youth mentoring, and mostly correlational.

sources.cite: Eby et al. 2008, JVB: does mentoring matter? meta-analysis

estress.name: Learn stress skills online
estress.promise: I'll learn the stress skills, one module at a time, and use them at work.
estress.core: Take a structured online course in stress skills (CBT- or mindfulness-based), one module at a time, and try one skill at work between modules.

light.text: Do one module every two weeks.

standard.text: Do one module a week for 6 to 7 weeks.

full.text: Do one module a week, and practice one skill each workday.

estress.ifThenExample: When I take my lunch break on a module day, I do my next module.

fitNotes.text: Ask HR or the employee assistance program; many employers pay for a course. Free evidence-based courses exist too.
Pick a guided version with a coach or check-ins; guided courses kept people going.
Pair it with a clinician; online courses work alongside care, not in place of it.
An app version fits between shifts; turn on the reminders.

notFor.reason: You're not in a job right now, so this one can wait.

estress.evidence: In 21 RCTs (5,260 employees), online psychological programs delivered at work improved wellbeing (g = 0.37) and work effectiveness (g = 0.25) right after the course; results varied a lot between studies and longer-term effects weren't measured. A WHO umbrella review rated the work-effectiveness result high certainty, its only high-certainty finding. Guided courses of 6–7 weeks with reminders kept people engaged best.

sources.cite: Carolan, Harris & Cavanagh 2017, JMIR: web-based psychological programs at work, 21 RCTs, n = 5,260
Miguel et al. 2023, Occup Environ Med: WHO umbrella review of workplace mental health interventions, 16 meta-analyses
Virtanen et al. 2025, Lancet Public Health: workplace health promotion, 88 meta-analyses

workcoach.name: Work with a coach
workcoach.promise: I'll get a coach in my corner and bring one decision to every session.
workcoach.core: Meet a trained work coach on a regular schedule, and leave each session with one goal to act on before the next.

light.text: Book one session, then a follow-up six weeks later.

standard.text: Meet monthly for six months.

full.text: Meet every two weeks, with an agreed action between sessions.

workcoach.ifThenExample: When I get to the first Wednesday of the month, I have my coaching session.

fitNotes.text: Ask whether your employer or its assistance program covers coaching; many do. Peer coaching with a colleague, taking turns, is free.
Try a business coach or a free small-business advising center; bring one decision to each session.
Pick a qualified coach; qualified coaches did better in the trials.
Try 45-minute video sessions.
Try a career coach, with sessions aimed at your search.

notFor.reason: You're not working right now, and the trials were with people in a job, so this one can wait.

workcoach.evidence: In 37 RCTs (2,528 people), workplace coaching improved leadership and personal outcomes by a moderate amount (g = 0.59). But the authors report significant publication bias, and effects were larger on self-ratings than on observed outcomes.

sources.cite: de Haan & Nilsson 2023, AMLE: workplace coaching, 37 RCTs, n = 2,528

careerrecord.name: Keep a career record
careerrecord.promise: I'll write down what I've done, so it's ready when the pressure's on.
careerrecord.core: Log your wins, feedback and new skills in one running document.

light.text: Update your record once a quarter.

standard.text: Update your record once a month.

full.text: Update your record every two weeks, with numbers attached to each win.

careerrecord.ifThenExample: When I wrap up the last Friday of the month, I update my career record.

fitNotes.text: Turn each entry into a resume bullet as you go.

careerrecord.evidence: A practical tactic with no direct trial. It feeds reviews, raise conversations and applications.

commitgoal.name: Lock savings to a goal
commitgoal.promise: I'll lock my savings to the thing I'm saving for.
commitgoal.core: Put savings for one named goal into an account you can't easily withdraw from until a set date or amount. Opening it is a one-time step; each deposit after that is the habit.

light.text: Lock one near goal toward what you're saving for, with a date 3 months out.

standard.text: Lock one goal with a date and amount, and automate the deposits.

full.text: Lock one goal per major priority, each one automated.

commitgoal.ifThenExample: When my pay lands, I move my set amount into the goal account.

ifThenExamplesFor.text: When a client payment clears, I move my set share into the goal account.

fitNotes.text: Pick a small, near goal, and keep an unlocked emergency buffer too.
A CD or a separate bank with no debit card works as a lock.
Name the account for the business. It keeps the money apart, and it's the first proof to yourself that it's real. Keep a separate, reachable fund for repairs and slow months too.

commitgoal.evidence: In an RCT with 1,777 bank clients in the Philippines, offering a commitment savings account raised average savings by 82% after a year. One trial, in one country.

sources.cite: Ashraf, Karlan & Yin 2006, QJE: commitment savings RCT (J-PAL summary)

experiences.name: Buy experiences, not things
experiences.promise: I'll spend on what I'll remember.
experiences.core: With spare spending money, pick shared experiences over things.

light.text: Swap one purchase for an experience each month.

standard.text: Before every non-essential purchase, ask what experience the money could buy.

full.text: Ask that before every non-essential purchase, and set a monthly experience budget.

experiences.ifThenExample: When I want to buy something non-essential, I ask what experience the same money could buy.

fitNotes.text: Free experiences count: a picnic, a hike, a free museum day with someone.
Pick experiences with other people; solo ones showed almost no advantage.
Before any non-essential purchase, wait 48 hours and ask what shared experience the same money could buy.

experiences.evidence: Across 141 studies, people were happier with experiential purchases than material ones (d = 0.38, about 0.23–0.27 after correcting for publication bias). The advantage mostly vanished for solo or bad experiences. The authors call the evidence largely correlational: most studies compared recalled purchases rather than testing a change in spending.

sources.cite: Weingarten & Goodman 2021, JCR: experiential advantage meta-analysis, 141 studies

futureself.name: Meet your future self
futureself.promise: I'll picture the person who lives with this decision before I make it.
futureself.core: Before a savings decision, picture the specific future you who will live with the result.

light.text: Do it once, when you set up automatic saving.

standard.text: Do it monthly, before your money review.

full.text: Do it monthly, and write a short letter from your 70-year-old self each year.

futureself.ifThenExample: When I set my savings rate, I open the aged photo of myself first.

fitNotes.text: Picture yourself 10 years out rather than at 70.

futureself.evidence: A 2025 systematic review of 23 randomized studies found future-self interventions shifted saving and health choices with small to large but mixed effects, mostly in young adults and mostly on lab or hypothetical tasks; only two tracked real behavior (pension sign-ups and exercise). The original age-progressed-image studies used students and hypothetical retirement allocations, not real saving.

sources.cite: Grekin et al. 2025: future self-continuity interventions, systematic review of 23 randomized studies
Hershfield et al. 2011, JMR: age-progressed renderings and saving

affirm.name: Values reflection
affirm.promise: I'll write about what matters most to me, and check my decisions against it.
affirm.core: Write briefly about your most important value and why it matters to you.

light.text: Once a month.

standard.text: Once a week.

full.text: Once a week, plus before any big decision.

affirm.ifThenExample: When I face a hard conversation or decision, I reread what I wrote about my top value first.

fitNotes.text: Three sentences are enough.
If it helps, sum it up as a one-line personal mission and check one decision a week against it.

affirm.evidence: In a 2025 meta-analysis of 129 tests (mostly US college students), brief self-affirmation exercises such as writing about core values raised general wellbeing (ES 0.29) and self-perception (0.32) over short follow-ups (about two weeks); only reductions in psychological barriers grew over time. An earlier analysis of 144 tests found a similar small effect on health behavior after health-risk messages (d = 0.32). Small effects, but a large and direct evidence base.

sources.cite: Zhang et al. 2025, American Psychologist: self-affirmation and wellbeing, 129 tests
Epton et al. 2015 / Harris et al.: self-affirmation and health behavior, 144 studies

threegood.name: Three good things
threegood.promise: I'll name three things that went well, and why, until I start noticing them on my own.
threegood.core: Write down three things that went well and why they happened.

light.text: Once a week.

standard.text: Three times a week.

full.text: Daily for two weeks, then weekly.

threegood.ifThenExample: When I get into bed, I write three good things.

fitNotes.text: Or share them with your partner instead of writing them down.

notFor.reason: You've had low mood most days, and gratitude exercises can feel invalidating then.

threegood.evidence: Gratitude exercises (mostly private lists and journals, some letters) had small effects on depressive symptoms across 27 studies (N = 3,675, mostly non-clinical adults); effects on anxiety were not significant. Effects were much larger against waitlists (g = −0.51) than active controls (g = −0.18), which suggests some placebo, and private and letter-style formats worked about equally.

sources.cite: Cregg & Cheavens 2021, J. Happiness Studies: gratitude and depression/anxiety

community.name: Spiritual or reflective community
community.promise: I'll show up somewhere that asks the big questions with me.
community.core: Go to a spiritual, religious or reflective community gathering on a regular schedule.

light.text: One gathering a month.

standard.text: One gathering every other week.

full.text: A weekly gathering, plus one service or volunteer role in the community.

community.ifThenExample: When I wake on a gathering Sunday, I head to my community gathering.

ifThenExamplesFor.text: When my day off lines up with a gathering, I go, in person or online.

fitNotes.text: Secular options count: a meditation center, humanist or ethical society, or a Quaker-style silent meeting.
Changing shifts? Online or midweek gatherings fit.

community.evidence: In 74,534 US nurses followed for about 20 years, attending religious services more than weekly went with 33% lower mortality than never attending, weekly with 26% lower, and less than weekly with 13% lower. Observational, and mostly white Christian women; social support accounted for about 23% of the link.

sources.cite: VanderWeele et al. 2016, JAMA Internal Medicine: religious service attendance and mortality

deeptalk.name: Go deeper in conversation
deeptalk.promise: I'll go deeper than small talk, one conversation at a time.
deeptalk.core: In one conversation, ask a question that goes past small talk, and share an honest answer too.

light.text: One deeper conversation a week.

standard.text: Two deeper conversations a week.

full.text: One a day, with someone new at least weekly.

deeptalk.ifThenExample: When I feel a conversation settle, I ask one real question: "What's been on your mind lately?"

fitNotes.text: Start with a service worker, a neighbor or a group member.
Try one question at dinner with your partner.

deeptalk.evidence: Across about a dozen experiments, people expected deep conversations with strangers to be more awkward and less enjoyable than they turned out to be; right afterward, they felt happier and more connected than they'd predicted. These were single lab conversations, with no longer-term follow-up.

sources.cite: Kardas, Kumar & Epley 2022, JPSP: miscalibrated expectations of deep conversation

creative.name: Make something
creative.promise: I'll make something, regularly, because making things is mine.
creative.core: Make something on a regular schedule: music, art, writing, dance or craft.

light.text: 30 minutes a week.

standard.text: Two sessions a week.

full.text: Three sessions a week, one of them with a group.

creative.ifThenExample: When I wrap up on Tuesday evening, I go to my art class.

fitNotes.text: A group class or choir matches how the trials were run.
Free library or community-center classes work, or a sketchbook and pencil.
Seated arts count: singing, drawing, writing, craft.

creative.evidence: In 39 controlled studies of older adults, group arts activities reduced depression (d = 0.70, about 0.42 after correcting for publication bias; 36 studies, 3,360 people) and anxiety (10 studies, 949 people). Results varied a lot between studies, and effects were about twice as large in care homes as in community settings. Evidence is strongest for older adults in groups.

sources.cite: 2024, Nature Mental Health: group arts for depression and anxiety in older adults, 39 studies

passiton.name: Pass it on
passiton.promise: I'll pass on what I know to someone coming up behind me.
passiton.core: Share your experience, skills or advice with someone younger or newer.

light.text: One piece of advice or help a month.

standard.text: Advice or help twice a month.

full.text: Advice or help weekly, or a regular mentoring role.

passiton.ifThenExample: When I sit down to plan my week, I pick who I'll pass one thing on to, and when.

ifThenExamplesFor.text: When I sit down to plan my week, I pick the newer colleague I'll pass one thing on to next.

fitNotes.text: At work: pick one newer colleague or lead and share the thing you wish someone had told you. It's mentoring before it's in your title.
No one in mind yet? Intergenerational programs (tutoring, reading with kids, apprenticeships) give you a built-in audience.
Keep a short list of the people you're bringing along, so each time is one name, not a decision.
Share with someone a few years behind: a student, a new hire, a younger sibling.

passiton.evidence: In a randomized trial of 73 older women, six weeks of writing life advice for middle-aged adults slightly reduced distress and increased social activity, with no change in loneliness; benefits faded by two months. A single small trial. For mentoring at work, a meta-analysis found mentors report slightly more job satisfaction and commitment than non-mentors (r ≈ .12); that link is correlational.

sources.cite: Moieni et al. 2020: randomized generativity intervention in older women
Ghosh & Reio 2013, Journal of Vocational Behavior: career benefits of mentoring for the mentors, meta-analysis

storyrec.name: Record one story
storyrec.promise: I'll tell my stories one at a time, and keep them where my family can find them.
storyrec.core: On a rhythm you keep, tell one story from your life into your phone as a voice memo: how something was done, who someone was, what a time taught you. Say at the start who it's for. Keep them all in one folder you share.

light.text: One 10-minute story every two weeks.

standard.text: One 15-minute story a week.

full.text: One story a week, plus sharing the folder with family once a month.

storyrec.ifThenExample: When I finish dinner on a story night, I record one story into my phone.

fitNotes.text: Tell it to someone at the table and let them ask questions; the questions pull out the parts you'd skip.
Ask a grandchild to hold the phone and ask the questions; they learn it by recording it.

storyrec.evidence: In a meta-analysis of 128 controlled trials, reminiscence programs (recalling and telling life stories, mostly with older adults) improved sense of integrity (g = 0.64) and depressive symptoms (g = 0.57), with smaller gains in purpose in life (g = 0.48); most effects held at follow-up. The trials were guided programs; recording on your own for family is a practical version of them, not the tested one.

sources.cite: Pinquart & Forstmeier 2012, Aging & Mental Health: reminiscence interventions, 128 controlled trials

yoga.name: Yoga practice
yoga.promise: I'll give my body and my head the same time on the mat.
yoga.core: Yoga (postures with steady breathing) on days you pick each week.

light.text: 15 minutes, twice a week.

standard.text: 30 minutes, twice a week.

full.text: 45 to 60 minutes, three times a week.

yoga.ifThenExample: When I finish dinner on Monday and Thursday evenings, I roll out the mat.

fitNotes.text: Chair or wall-supported yoga; skip any pose that hurts the joint.
Seated or adaptive yoga; skip anything that loads sore shoulders.
Skip poses that load the hands and shoulders (planks, downward dog); forearms or a chair instead.
Gentle or chair yoga classes built for older adults count.
A class adds company; many studios run free community sessions.
Free video classes and a towel instead of a mat work fine.
15-minute sessions count.

safety.text: A quick go-ahead from your doctor or physical therapist first, so you can build without guessing.

yoga.evidence: In a network meta-analysis of 183 RCTs (22,811 adults without diagnosed conditions), yoga had among the larger effects on wellbeing (SMD 0.49) versus mostly inactive or waitlist controls, though differences between interventions weren't significant and 60% of trials were at high risk of bias. The 2024 BMJ analysis of people with depression also found yoga among the most effective (g = −0.55 vs active controls) and best-tolerated exercise, with very low certainty.

sources.cite: 2025 network meta-analysis, Nature Human Behaviour: wellbeing interventions, 183 RCTs
Noetel et al. 2024, BMJ: exercise for depression, network meta-analysis

worry.name: Worry time
worry.promise: I'll give my worries an appointment instead of my whole day.
worry.core: When a worry shows up, jot it down and save it for a set daily worry period.

light.text: Postpone one worry a day to a 10-minute worry period.

standard.text: Postpone all worries to one daily 15-minute worry period.

full.text: A daily worry period, plus one action step written for each solvable worry.

worry.ifThenExample: When a worry shows up, I jot it in one line and let it wait; at 6 p.m., I open the list for my worry time.

fitNotes.text: Set the worry period well before your main sleep, not right before it.
A voice memo works as the list.
Try a commute or a quiet moment after school drop-off.

worry.evidence: In 7 randomized trials (999 people), worry postponement practiced for one to four weeks cut the duration (d = 0.31) and frequency (d = 0.19) of daily worry. Small effects; long-term follow-up is lacking.

sources.cite: Dippel et al. 2023, Int J Cognitive Therapy: worry postponement meta-analysis, 7 trials

coaching.name: Work with a financial coach
coaching.promise: I'll get a coach for my money and leave every session with one action.
coaching.core: Meet a financial coach or nonprofit counselor on a regular schedule and leave each session with one money action.

light.text: Book one session, then a 3-month check-in.

standard.text: Meet monthly for 6 months.

full.text: Meet monthly, plus a short weekly check-in by message.

coaching.ifThenExample: When I get to the first Tuesday of the month, I have my coaching call.

fitNotes.text: Free options: nonprofit credit counseling, credit-union or bank coaching, or a local financial empowerment center.
Try a fee-only planner (paid by the hour, not by commission).
Phone or video sessions work.

coaching.evidence: In the first randomized evaluation of financial coaching (two US sites), coaching improved savings and credit scores at one site and cut total debt and delinquencies at the other, along with money management and perceived financial wellbeing.

sources.cite: Theodos et al. 2018: randomized evaluation of financial coaching

reminders.name: Payday goal reminder
reminders.promise: I'll remind myself on payday what I'm saving for.
reminders.core: Set a recurring reminder that names the specific thing you're saving for.

light.text: Set one reminder a month on payday.

standard.text: Set a reminder every payday naming the goal and amount.

full.text: Set a payday reminder, plus a monthly progress update toward the goal.

reminders.ifThenExample: When I see my "Car fund: this week" reminder on payday, I move the money.

fitNotes.text: If your pay varies and automation isn't possible, this does the job of an automatic transfer.
Name a near, concrete goal, like "a one-week emergency buffer".

reminders.evidence: In three field RCTs with 14,167 bank clients (Bolivia, Peru, the Philippines), monthly bank reminders raised savings about 6%, a marginal result; in Peru, reminders naming the client's own savings goal raised them about 16%, while generic ones did nothing. In a 2025 megastudy of 1.9 million US bank customers, generic reminder emails raised the chance of a deposit by only 0.05 percentage points on average (0.13 at best). Goal-naming reminders have the most support; self-set reminders weren't tested.

sources.cite: Karlan et al. 2016, Management Science: reminders and saving, 3 field RCTs
Milkman et al. 2025, PNAS Nexus: savings reminder megastudy, n = 1,925,785

actprog.name: Self-help ACT program
actprog.promise: I'll work through the program that teaches me to act on what I value.
actprog.core: Work through a structured self-help Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT) program, a book or app, covering values, acceptance and committed action.

light.text: One exercise every two weeks.

standard.text: One chapter or module a week for 8 weeks.

full.text: One module a week, plus a daily 5-minute practice.

actprog.ifThenExample: When I sit down on a Sunday afternoon, I do my next ACT exercise.

fitNotes.text: Library books and free ACT apps are enough.
If you can, pair it with a clinician; guided versions worked better.

actprog.evidence: In 13 RCTs (2,580 people), self-help ACT improved depression (g = 0.34), anxiety (g = 0.35) and psychological flexibility (g = 0.42). More clinician guidance improved results; the authors call conclusions tentative.

sources.cite: French et al. 2017, JCBS: self-help ACT meta-analysis, 13 RCTs
